name: Concrete Jungle
subject: New York City
tagline: Eleven questions on the city most of you left on Friday: boroughs, bridges, bagels and the bits you walk past every day. Starts easy, ends hard.

questions.q: How many boroughs make up New York City?
questions.w: Five: Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island, joined into one city in 1898.
questions.more: Brooklyn was the third-largest city in America in its own right before the merger, which its newspapers called the Great Mistake of 1898. Queens is the largest borough by area and the most diverse place in the country, with around 160 languages spoken. Staten Islanders voted to secede in 1993 and the state never acted on it.

questions.q: Which Manhattan park, 843 acres of it, was laid out by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux in the 1850s?
questions.w: Central Park, the first landscaped public park in the United States, built on swamp, rock and the cleared Black village of Seneca Village.
questions.more: Olmsted and Vaux won the design competition in 1858 and later did Prospect Park in Brooklyn, which they considered their better work. The park's lamp posts carry numbers that tell you the nearest cross street. About 42 million people visit a year, more than any other urban park in the country.

questions.q: Which bridge, finished in 1883, was the longest suspension bridge in the world and is now the one with the wooden walkway full of tourists?
questions.w: The Brooklyn Bridge, designed by John Roebling, who died before construction began, and finished by his son Washington and daughter-in-law Emily.
questions.more: Washington Roebling was crippled by the bends from working in the underwater caissons and oversaw the rest from his window with a telescope while Emily carried his instructions to the site and learned the engineering herself. A week after opening, a rumour that it was collapsing caused a stampede that killed twelve people. P. T. Barnum walked 21 elephants across it to prove it was safe.

questions.q: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from which country?
questions.w: France, designed by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi with an iron skeleton by Gustave Eiffel, and dedicated in 1886.
questions.more: The French paid for the statue and the Americans had to pay for the pedestal, which stalled until the publisher Joseph Pulitzer shamed the public into sending 120,000 small donations. Her copper skin is the thickness of two pennies and was brown when she arrived; the green patina took about thirty years. She is officially in New York but the island is nearer New Jersey.

questions.q: What do New Yorkers call the subway line that runs under Lexington Avenue, the most crowded in the country?
questions.w: The 4, 5 and 6, the Lexington Avenue line, which carries more riders a day than the entire Washington Metro.
questions.more: The Second Avenue Subway was proposed in 1920 to relieve it and the first three stations finally opened on New Year's Day 2017. The 7 is the Flushing line through Queens, the L goes to Williamsburg, and the A, C and E run down the West Side. The subway has run 24 hours a day since 1904, one of very few systems in the world that never closes.

questions.q: New Amsterdam became New York in 1664 when the Dutch handed it to the English without a fight. The city was renamed for whom?
o: The Duke of York, the king's brother
The city of York in England
questions.w: James, Duke of York, brother of Charles II, who had been granted the land. He later became King James II.
questions.more: The Dutch governor Peter Stuyvesant wanted to fight but the townspeople, including his own son, signed a petition telling him to surrender. In 1667 the Dutch swapped their claim for the nutmeg island of Run in Indonesia and the sugar colony of Suriname, and thought they had the better deal. Harlem, Brooklyn and the Bowery are all Dutch names.

questions.q: The New York bagel is boiled before it is baked. What do locals insist makes it better than anywhere else's?
questions.w: The water, piped unfiltered from reservoirs in the Catskills, soft and low in minerals.
questions.more: Bakers elsewhere have installed systems to copy the chemistry, which suggests there is something to it, though blind tests mostly find technique matters more. The water comes 125 miles through tunnels so well built that the city has run on them for a century; a third tunnel, started in 1970, is still being finished. The same water gets credit for the pizza.

questions.q: Which Manhattan building, finished in 1930, was the tallest in the world for eleven months and still has its eagle-head gargoyles and Art Deco crown?
questions.w: The Chrysler Building, which won a race to the top by assembling its 56-metre steel spire inside the building and hoisting it out in 90 minutes.
questions.more: Its rival, 40 Wall Street, had thought it had won. The gargoyles are modelled on the Chrysler cars' radiator caps and hood ornaments of 1929. Walter Chrysler paid for it himself so his children could inherit it, and the company never actually owned it. New Yorkers regularly vote it their favourite skyscraper.

questions.q: The oldest bar in the city, with sawdust on the floor and a rule against women that lasted until a court order in 1970, is which?
questions.w: McSorley's on East 7th Street, open since 1854 by its own account, serving only its light and dark ale, two mugs at a time.
questions.more: Its motto was 'Good ale, raw onions and no ladies'. Abraham Lincoln is said to have drunk there, and the wishbones hanging over the bar were left by soldiers going off to the First World War, to be collected when they came back. Fraunces Tavern downtown is older as a building, where Washington said farewell to his officers in 1783, but it has not been a bar continuously.

questions.q: The famous blackout of July 1977 hit the city in the middle of a heatwave and a serial-killer scare. What was the killer calling himself?
questions.w: Son of Sam, David Berkowitz, who was arrested that August after a parking ticket placed his car near a shooting.
questions.more: The blackout lasted 25 hours and set off looting and arson across the Bronx and Brooklyn, with more than 3,000 arrests, and became the symbol of the city's near-bankrupt 1970s. Hip-hop lore says looted turntables and mixers seeded a wave of new DJs in the Bronx. The Yankees won the World Series that October, the summer that gave the city the phrase 'Bronx Zoo'.

questions.q: Which of these are in Brooklyn? Select all that apply.
questions.w: Coney Island, Prospect Park and the Barclays Center are in Brooklyn. Yankee Stadium is in the Bronx and Flushing Meadows, home of the US Open and the Mets, is in Queens.
questions.more: Coney Island's Cyclone roller coaster has run since 1927 and its Nathan's hot-dog eating contest every Fourth of July since, the owners claim, 1916. The Barclays Center opened in 2012 on a site that took a decade of lawsuits to clear and brought the Nets back to Brooklyn, which had lost the Dodgers to Los Angeles in 1957 and never forgave anyone.
